claim: The Drosophila adult brain contains approximately 100,000 neurons.
source: With an extended genetic toolkit and a brain of only ∼100,000 neurons (Raji and Potter, 2021; Alivisatos et al., 2012) largely reconstructed at the EM level (Zheng et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020a), Drosophila represents an attractive system to provide experimental evidence on the mechanisms behind pattern separation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Raji and Potter, 2021 and Alivisatos et al., 2012.

claim: The Drosophila brain has been largely reconstructed at the electron microscopy level.
source: With an extended genetic toolkit and a brain of only ∼100,000 neurons (Raji and Potter, 2021; Alivisatos et al., 2012) largely reconstructed at the EM level (Zheng et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020a), Drosophila represents an attractive system to provide experimental evidence on the mechanisms behind pattern separation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to EM reconstruction studies (Zheng et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020a).

claim: The Drosophila mushroom body is required for memory formation and retrieval.
source: The MB is required for memory formation and retrieval (Heisenberg et al., 1985; de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994; Dubnau et al., 2001; McGuire et al., 2001; Aso et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating the MB's role in memory (Heisenberg et al., 1985; de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994; Dubnau et al., 2001; McGuire et al., 2001; Aso et al., 2014).

claim: The Drosophila mushroom body receives mainly olfactory input, though optical, temperature, and humidity information is also represented.
source: The fly MB receives mainly olfactory input, though optical, temperature, and humidity information is also represented (Marin, 2020; Frank et al., 2015; Li et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing different types of sensory input to the MB (Marin, 2020; Frank et al., 2015; Li et al., 2020b).

claim: There are 51 distinct olfactory glomeruli in the Drosophila antennal lobe.
source: Within the MB input region, in the main calyx, olfactory projection neurons (PNs) deliver sensory information from 51 distinct olfactory glomeruli (Grabe et al., 2016; Bates et al., 2020) to ∼2000 Kenyon cells (KCs) of the MB (Aso et al., 2009), for an expansion ratio of 40 (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grabe et al., 2016 and Bates et al., 2020.

claim: The Drosophila mushroom body contains approximately 2000 Kenyon cells.
source: Within the MB input region, in the main calyx, olfactory projection neurons (PNs) deliver sensory information from 51 distinct olfactory glomeruli (Grabe et al., 2016; Bates et al., 2020) to ∼2000 Kenyon cells (KCs) of the MB (Aso et al., 2009), for an expansion ratio of 40 (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Aso et al., 2009.

claim: The expansion ratio from projection neurons to Kenyon cells in the Drosophila mushroom body is 40.
source: Within the MB input region, in the main calyx, olfactory projection neurons (PNs) deliver sensory information from 51 distinct olfactory glomeruli (Grabe et al., 2016; Bates et al., 2020) to ∼2000 Kenyon cells (KCs) of the MB (Aso et al., 2009), for an expansion ratio of 40 (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017.

claim: In the mushroom body calyx, projection neurons synapse onto Kenyon cells via complex synaptic structures known as microglomeruli.
source: In the calyx, PNs synapse onto KCs via complex synaptic structures known as microglomeruli (MGs) (Yasuyama et al., 2002; Kremer et al., 2010; Leiss et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies describing microglomeruli (Yasuyama et al., 2002; Kremer et al., 2010; Leiss et al., 2009).

claim: At each microglomerulus, a single central projection neuron bouton is enwrapped by, on average, 13 claw-like dendritic terminals of as many different Kenyon cells.
source: At each MG, a single central PN bouton is enwrapped by, on average, 13 claw-like dendritic terminals of as many different KCs (Davi D Bock, personal communication).
evidence: The claim is supported by a personal communication from Davi D Bock.

claim: Each Kenyon cell receives input from six to eight projection neurons, on average.
source: KCs integrate inputs in a combinatorial manner, with each KC receiving input from six to eight PNs, on average (Butcher et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020a; Turner et al., 2008), of which more than half need to be coactive to elicit spikes (Gruntman and Turner, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Butcher et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020a; Turner et al., 2008).

claim: More than half of the projection neuron inputs to a Kenyon cell need to be coactive to elicit spikes.
source: KCs integrate inputs in a combinatorial manner, with each KC receiving input from six to eight PNs, on average (Butcher et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020a; Turner et al., 2008), of which more than half need to be coactive to elicit spikes (Gruntman and Turner, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gruntman and Turner, 2013.

claim: Projection neuron odour-evoked activity is broadly tuned.
source: As a result, while PN odour-evoked activity is broadly tuned (Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Bhandawat et al., 2007), odour representation is sparse and decorrelated at the KCs layer (Honegger et al., 2011; Turner et al., 2008; Campbell et al., 2013; Perez-Orive et al., 2002), therefore reducing overlap between stimuli representation and allowing for better discriminability (Kanerva, 1988; Cayco-Gajic et al., 2017; Olshausen and Field, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Perez-Orive et al., 2002 and Bhandawat et al., 2007.

claim: Odour representation is sparse and decorrelated at the Kenyon cells layer.
source: As a result, while PN odour-evoked activity is broadly tuned (Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Bhandawat et al., 2007), odour representation is sparse and decorrelated at the KCs layer (Honegger et al., 2011; Turner et al., 2008; Campbell et al., 2013; Perez-Orive et al., 2002), therefore reducing overlap between stimuli representation and allowing for better discriminability (Kanerva, 1988; Cayco-Gajic et al., 2017; Olshausen and Field, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Honegger et al., 2011; Turner et al., 2008; Campbell et al., 2013; Perez-Orive et al., 2002).

claim: Sparse and decorrelated odour representation at the Kenyon cells layer reduces overlap between stimuli representation and allows for better discriminability.
source: As a result, while PN odour-evoked activity is broadly tuned (Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Bhandawat et al., 2007), odour representation is sparse and decorrelated at the KCs layer (Honegger et al., 2011; Turner et al., 2008; Campbell et al., 2013; Perez-Orive et al., 2002), therefore reducing overlap between stimuli representation and allowing for better discriminability (Kanerva, 1988; Cayco-Gajic et al., 2017; Olshausen and Field, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to theoretical work (Kanerva, 1988; Cayco-Gajic et al., 2017; Olshausen and Field, 2004).

claim: Inhibition is required to reduce the overlap among odour representations in the Drosophila mushroom body.
source: In addition to sparse PN:KC connectivity and KCs high input threshold, inhibition is required to reduce the overlap among odour representations in the Drosophila MB (Lin et al., 2014; Lei et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lin et al., 2014 and Lei et al., 2013.

claim: The GABAergic anterior paired lateral (APL) neuron provides inhibition at the mushroom body.
source: At the MB, inhibition is provided by the GABAergic anterior paired lateral (APL) neuron, which innervates both the calyx and the lobes of the MB (Liu and Davis, 2009; Pitman et al., 2011; Aso et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu and Davis, 2009; Pitman et al., 2011; Aso et al., 2014.

claim: The APL neuron innervates both the calyx and the lobes of the mushroom body.
source: At the MB, inhibition is provided by the GABAergic anterior paired lateral (APL) neuron, which innervates both the calyx and the lobes of the MB (Liu and Davis, 2009; Pitman et al., 2011; Aso et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu and Davis, 2009; Pitman et al., 2011; Aso et al., 2014.

claim: APL responds to odours with depolarization and calcium influx.
source: APL responds to odours with depolarization and calcium influx (Liu and Davis, 2009; Papadopoulou et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu and Davis, 2009 and Papadopoulou et al., 2011.

claim: Blocking APL output disrupts the sparse odour representation in Kenyon cells.
source: Importantly, blocking APL output disrupts the KCs sparse odour representation and impairs learned discrimination of similar odours, pointing to its critical role in the process (Lin et al., 2014; Lei et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lin et al., 2014 and Lei et al., 2013.

claim: Blocking APL output impairs learned discrimination of similar odours.
source: Importantly, blocking APL output disrupts the KCs sparse odour representation and impairs learned discrimination of similar odours, pointing to its critical role in the process (Lin et al., 2014; Lei et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lin et al., 2014 and Lei et al., 2013.

claim: APL is both pre- and postsynaptic to projection neurons and Kenyon cells in the adult calyx.
source: However, APL is both pre- and postsynaptic to PNs and KCs in the adult calyx (Yasuyama et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2013; Baltruschat et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yasuyama et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2013; Baltruschat et al., 2021.

claim: APL response to localized stimuli is spatially restricted.
source: Additionally, APL response to localized stimuli is spatially restricted (Amin et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Amin et al., 2020.

claim: APL branches at the mushroom body lobes and the ones in the calyx appear to represent two separate compartments.
source: In particular, APL branches at the MB lobes and the ones in the calyx appear to represent two separate compartments (Amin et al., 2020), suggesting a possible distinct role of APL inhibition in these two different compartments.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Amin et al., 2020.

claim: Out of the 136 projection neurons reported innervating the main calyx, 126 made and received synapses with APL.
source: Out of the 136 PNs reported innervating the main calyx (Li et al., 2020a), 126 made and received synapses with APL (full list of PNs and APL interactions available at: https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.bk3j9kdd1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis from the hemibrain EM dataset and citation to Li et al., 2020a.

claim: 84% ± 2% of APL-to-PN connections are localized on projection neuron boutons.
source: Most of the APL-to-PN connections were localized on PN boutons (84% ± 2%, mean ± SEM, of the total synapses received by each PN localized on boutons), demonstrating that the majority of APL-PN interactions happens at MGs (Figure 1B, all images available at: https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.bk3j9kdd1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of EM data from the hemibrain dataset.

claim: The majority of APL-PN interactions happen at microglomeruli.
source: Most of the APL-to-PN connections were localized on PN boutons (84% ± 2%, mean ± SEM, of the total synapses received by each PN localized on boutons), demonstrating that the majority of APL-PN interactions happens at MGs (Figure 1B, all images available at: https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.bk3j9kdd1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that most APL-to-PN connections are on PN boutons, which are the central structures of microglomeruli.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the number of synapses made by APL towards a specific projection neuron and the reciprocal synapses formed by that projection neuron onto APL.
source: To test whether the contribution of APL would be dependent on the input weight, defined as the total number of synapses received by APL from a particular input, we plotted the weight of APL-to-PN synapses against the PN-to-APL one. We found a positive correlation between the number of synapses made by APL towards a specific PN and the reciprocal synapses formed by that PN onto APL (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1D, which displays a correlation (r2 = 0.63).

claim: Of the 1919 Kenyon cells present in the hemibrain dataset, 1871 displayed interactions with APL in the calyx.
source: Similarly, of the 1919 KCs present in the dataset, 1871 displayed interactions with APL in the calyx.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis from the hemibrain EM dataset.

claim: APL synapses onto α/β Kenyon cells were significantly less localized on claw-like dendritic terminals and more distributed along KC dendritic branches compared to other KC types.
source: We found a difference in the spatial distribution of APL synapses depending on the KC type, suggesting that APL inhibition might have a different impact on different KC types. In particular, APL synapses onto α/β KCs were significantly less localized on claw-like dendritic terminals and more distributed along KC dendritic branches (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, n = 210 [70 per KC type, randomly selected], p < 0.0001, unpaired ANOVA with multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of EM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C with statistical testing (n = 210, p < 0.0001).

claim: The number of KC-to-APL synapses positively correlates with the APL-to-KC synapse number.
source: As in the case of PNs, the number of KC-to-APL synapses positively correlated with the APL-to-KC synapse number (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1E, which displays a correlation (r2 = 0.60).

claim: APL displays different response levels to different odours in the calyx.
source: Odour-elicited calcium transients in APL were detectable in the calyx (Figure 2B and E). Interestingly, we observed a clear difference in the GCaMP fluorescence levels, measured as ΔF/F0 over the entire calycal region innervated by APL (see also Materials and methods) in response to the two odour stimulations, with Oct eliciting a stronger APL response (Figure 2C–D, n = 10, p = 0.002, Wilcoxon matched-pairs test).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data showing differential APL responses to Mch vs. Oct (n = 10, p = 0.002).

claim: 3-octanol elicits a stronger APL response compared to 4-methylcyclohexanol in the calyx.
source: Interestingly, we observed a clear difference in the GCaMP fluorescence levels, measured as ΔF/F0 over the entire calycal region innervated by APL (see also Materials and methods) in response to the two odour stimulations, with Oct eliciting a stronger APL response (Figure 2C–D, n = 10, p = 0.002, Wilcoxon matched-pairs test).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data (n = 10, p = 0.002).

claim: 3-octanol elicits a stronger APL response compared to δ-decalactone in the calyx.
source: Similarly, we measured a difference between the strength of the response to Oct compared to δ-DL (Figure 2F–G, n = 10, p < 0.0001, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data (n = 10, p < 0.0001).

claim: The gap between the δ-decalactone signal peak and the 3-octanol peak in APL was higher compared to the 4-methylcyclohexanol vs. 3-octanol group.
source: Moreover, the gap between the δ-DL signal peak and the Oct one was higher compared to the Mch vs. Oct group (Δ(Oct-Mch) = 45% ± 27%; Δ(Oct-δ-DL) = 76% ± 30%, n = 10, p = 0.0234, unpaired t-test with Welch correction), suggesting that APL is able to provide a variable, odour-tuned inhibition to MGs of the MB calyx.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison of calcium imaging data (n = 10, p = 0.0234).

claim: APL is able to provide a variable, odour-tuned inhibition to microglomeruli of the mushroom body calyx.
source: Moreover, the gap between the δ-DL signal peak and the Oct one was higher compared to the Mch vs. Oct group (Δ(Oct-Mch) = 45% ± 27%; Δ(Oct-δ-DL) = 76% ± 30%, n = 10, p = 0.0234, unpaired t-test with Welch correction), suggesting that APL is able to provide a variable, odour-tuned inhibition to MGs of the MB calyx.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that APL shows different response levels to different odours.

claim: The number of responding glomeruli in projection neurons was similar between 4-methylcyclohexanol and 3-octanol stimulations.
source: While the number of responding glomeruli was similar between the two tested odours (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, also shown on a larger number of AL glomeruli in Barth et al., 2014), the overall calcium transient was higher when flies were exposed to Oct (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B, n = 10, p = 0.002, Wilcoxon matched-pairs test), suggesting that the main source of difference was represented by the degree of PNs activation rather than an additional/decreased number of active neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The overall calcium transient in projection neuron dendrites was higher when flies were exposed to 3-octanol compared to 4-methylcyclohexanol.
source: While the number of responding glomeruli was similar between the two tested odours (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, also shown on a larger number of AL glomeruli in Barth et al., 2014), the overall calcium transient was higher when flies were exposed to Oct (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B, n = 10, p = 0.002, Wilcoxon matched-pairs test), suggesting that the main source of difference was represented by the degree of PNs activation rather than an additional/decreased number of active neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data (n = 10, p = 0.002).

claim: The main source of difference in projection neuron activity between odours is the degree of activation rather than the number of active neurons.
source: While the number of responding glomeruli was similar between the two tested odours (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, also shown on a larger number of AL glomeruli in Barth et al., 2014), the overall calcium transient was higher when flies were exposed to Oct (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B, n = 10, p = 0.002, Wilcoxon matched-pairs test), suggesting that the main source of difference was represented by the degree of PNs activation rather than an additional/decreased number of active neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the number of responding glomeruli is similar but the overall calcium transient differs.

claim: The number of active projection neuron boutons was similar between 4-methylcyclohexanol and 3-octanol stimulations.
source: While the number of active boutons was similar between Mch and Oct stimulations (Figure 3D, n = 10, p = 0.689, paired t-test), the average response peak among active boutons was higher when flies were exposed to Oct (Figure 3B, n = 10, p = 0.0002, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data with statistical testing (n = 10, p = 0.689).

claim: The average response peak among active projection neuron boutons was higher when flies were exposed to 3-octanol compared to 4-methylcyclohexanol.
source: While the number of active boutons was similar between Mch and Oct stimulations (Figure 3D, n = 10, p = 0.689, paired t-test), the average response peak among active boutons was higher when flies were exposed to Oct (Figure 3B, n = 10, p = 0.0002, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data with statistical testing (n = 10, p = 0.0002).

claim: The frequency distribution of all projection neuron boutons activity peaks showed a clear shift towards higher values for the 3-octanol-responding population compared to 4-methylcyclohexanol.
source: Furthermore, plotting the frequency distribution of all boutons activity peaks measured during these experiments showed a clear shift towards higher values of the entire Oct-responding population (Figure 3C, n = 10, p < 0.0001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency distribution analysis with statistical testing (n = 10, p < 0.0001).

claim: The overall level of projection neuron activation elicited by different odours correlated with the calycal APL response to those odours.
source: Taken together, these data suggested that APL neuron activation scales with PN inputs strength. Indeed, while further odours will be needed to reach a more general conclusion, the overall level of PN activation elicited by Mch, Oct, or δ-DL correlated with the calycal APL response to those odours (Pearson's r correlation coefficient between APL activity in Figure 2D and G and PN activity in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, D = 0.95).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis (Pearson's r = 0.95) between PN and APL activity data.

claim: APL neuron activation scales with projection neuron input strength.
source: Taken together, these data suggested that APL neuron activation scales with PN inputs strength. Indeed, while further odours will be needed to reach a more general conclusion, the overall level of PN activation elicited by Mch, Oct, or δ-DL correlated with the calycal APL response to those odours (Pearson's r correlation coefficient between APL activity in Figure 2D and G and PN activity in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, D = 0.95).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the high correlation (r = 0.95) between PN activation and APL response.

claim: The average activity peak among responding Kenyon cell claws was comparable between 4-methylcyclohexanol and 3-octanol exposures.
source: Importantly, the average postsynaptic response among MGs active in each odour trial was not different when comparing the response to Mch vs. Oct stimulation (Figure 3F, n = 9, p = 0.1648, paired t-test) or δ-DL vs. Oct stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F, n = 10, p = 0.767, Wilcoxon matched-pairs test).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data with statistical testing (n = 9, p = 0.1648).

claim: The average activity peak among responding Kenyon cell claws was comparable between δ-decalactone and 3-octanol exposures.
source: Importantly, the average postsynaptic response among MGs active in each odour trial was not different when comparing the response to Mch vs. Oct stimulation (Figure 3F, n = 9, p = 0.1648, paired t-test) or δ-DL vs. Oct stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F, n = 10, p = 0.767, Wilcoxon matched-pairs test).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data with statistical testing (n = 10, p = 0.767).

claim: The frequency distributions of odour-evoked activity peaks in Kenyon cell claws were overlapping between 4-methylcyclohexanol and 3-octanol.
source: Additionally, the frequency distributions of the odour-evoked activity peaks were overlapping (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 2G, n = 9–10, p = 0.0982 and p = 0.9554 for Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2G, respectively, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency distribution analysis with statistical testing (n = 9, p = 0.0982).

claim: The distance between 3-octanol- and 4-methylcyclohexanol-induced activity in Kenyon cell claws was significantly lower compared to the one measured in projection neuron boutons.
source: Finally, the distance between the Oct- and Mch-induced activity in KC claws was significantly lower compared to the one measured in PN boutons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, n = 10, p = 0.0271, Brown-Forsythe and Welch ANOVA test with multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis with statistical testing (n = 10, p = 0.0271).

claim: The differences in activation strength at the input population of microglomeruli (the projection neuron boutons) are normalized at the next neuronal layer, in the Kenyon cell claw-like dendritic endings.
source: Hence, the differences in activation strength described at the input population of MGs (the PN boutons) seemed to be normalized at the next neuronal layer, in the KC claw-like dendritic endings.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PN boutons show variable responses while KC claws show more uniform responses.

claim: The range of postsynaptic responses in microglomeruli appears to be restrained.
source: Thus, the range of postsynaptic responses in MGs appears to be restrained.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that KC claw responses are more uniform than PN bouton responses.

claim: In control animals with active APL, the average activity peak among responding microglomeruli did not show a difference between 4-methylcyclohexanol and 3-octanol stimulation.
source: As expected, control animals did not show a difference in the average activity peak among responding MGs (Figure 4B, n = 10, p = 0.949, two-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons) or in the number of responding units (Figure 4D, n = 10, p = 0.995, two-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data with statistical testing (n = 10, p = 0.949).

claim: In control animals with active APL, the number of responding microglomeruli did not differ between 4-methylcyclohexanol and 3-octanol stimulation.
source: As expected, control animals did not show a difference in the average activity peak among responding MGs (Figure 4B, n = 10, p = 0.949, two-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons) or in the number of responding units (Figure 4D, n = 10, p = 0.995, two-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data with statistical testing (n = 10, p = 0.995).

claim: In calyces where APL output was blocked, there was a significant difference in the response to 4-methylcyclohexanol and 3-octanol, with 3-octanol causing a stronger average odour-evoked activity.
source: In calyces where the APL output was blocked by TNT expression though, we measured a significant difference in the response to the two tested odours, with Oct causing a stronger average odour-evoked activity (Figure 4B, n = 10, p = 0.0003, two-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons) as well as a slight increase in the number of responding MGs (Figure 4D, n = 10, p = 0.047, two-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data with statistical testing (n = 10, p = 0.0003).

claim: In calyces where APL output was blocked, there was a slight increase in the number of responding microglomeruli for 3-octanol compared to 4-methylcyclohexanol.
source: In calyces where the APL output was blocked by TNT expression though, we measured a significant difference in the response to the two tested odours, with Oct causing a stronger average odour-evoked activity (Figure 4B, n = 10, p = 0.0003, two-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons) as well as a slight increase in the number of responding MGs (Figure 4D, n = 10, p = 0.047, two-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data with statistical testing (n = 10, p = 0.047).

claim: Small clusters of responding microglomeruli were often found spatially close to each other in the APL OFF scenarios.
source: Interestingly, small clusters of responding MGs were often found spatially close to each other in the APL OFF scenarios (e.g., compare spatial distribution of Oct responders in 4C vs. 4A) suggesting a possible locality of APL-mediated inhibition.
evidence: The claim is based on qualitative observation of imaging data comparing APL ON and APL OFF conditions.

claim: The frequency distribution of microglomeruli responses in APL OFF flies showed two shifted populations, with 3-octanol responses skewed towards higher values.
source: Finally, the frequency distribution plot for the APL OFF flies showed two shifted populations, with Oct responses skewed towards higher values (Figure 4F, n = 10, p < 0.0001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test), resembling the distribution displayed by the PN boutons (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency distribution analysis with statistical testing (n = 10, p < 0.0001).

claim: In the absence of APL output, the frequency distribution of Kenyon cell claw responses resembles the distribution displayed by projection neuron boutons.
source: Finally, the frequency distribution plot for the APL OFF flies showed two shifted populations, with Oct responses skewed towards higher values (Figure 4F, n = 10, p < 0.0001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test), resembling the distribution displayed by the PN boutons (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of frequency distributions between APL OFF KC claws and PN boutons.

claim: Blocking APL output leads to a more variable odour representation at the level of Kenyon cell claws.
source: In summary, blocking APL output led to a more variable odour representation at the level of KC claws.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that APL OFF conditions result in differential KC claw responses to different odours, similar to PN boutons.

claim: The more variable odour representation in Kenyon cell claws when APL is blocked bears a higher similarity to the activity of the input population.
source: This variable odour representation bore a higher similarity to the activity of the input population, hence supporting the hypothesis that APL acts as an input strength normalizer on MGs in the MB calyx.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of KC claw responses in APL OFF conditions to PN bouton responses.

claim: APL acts as an input strength normalizer on microglomeruli in the mushroom body calyx.
source: This variable odour representation bore a higher similarity to the activity of the input population, hence supporting the hypothesis that APL acts as an input strength normalizer on MGs in the MB calyx.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations that APL response scales with PN input, KC claw responses are normalized when APL is active, and blocking APL leads to variable KC responses similar to PN responses.

claim: Pentyl acetate activates the glomerulus DM3, whose projection neurons terminate in the posterior part of the calyx mainly.
source: Based on an available database of odorant representations (Münch and Galizia, 2016), these PNs are activated by the following odours: Pentyl acetate (PA) activates the glomerulus DM3, whose PNs terminate in the posterior part of the calyx mainly; methyl palmitate (MP) activates the glomerulus VA1d, whose PN terminals populate the anterior part of the calyx; farnesol (FA) activates glomerulus DC3, with PN terminals that populate the anterior part of the calyx, similarly to VA1d (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an odorant representation database (Münch and Galizia, 2016) and confirmed by EM data visualization.

claim: Methyl palmitate activates the glomerulus VA1d, whose projection neuron terminals populate the anterior part of the calyx.
source: Based on an available database of odorant representations (Münch and Galizia, 2016), these PNs are activated by the following odours: Pentyl acetate (PA) activates the glomerulus DM3, whose PNs terminate in the posterior part of the calyx mainly; methyl palmitate (MP) activates the glomerulus VA1d, whose PN terminals populate the anterior part of the calyx; farnesol (FA) activates glomerulus DC3, with PN terminals that populate the anterior part of the calyx, similarly to VA1d (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an odorant representation database (Münch and Galizia, 2016) and confirmed by EM data visualization.

claim: Farnesol activates glomerulus DC3, with projection neuron terminals that populate the anterior part of the calyx.
source: Based on an available database of odorant representations (Münch and Galizia, 2016), these PNs are activated by the following odours: Pentyl acetate (PA) activates the glomerulus DM3, whose PNs terminate in the posterior part of the calyx mainly; methyl palmitate (MP) activates the glomerulus VA1d, whose PN terminals populate the anterior part of the calyx; farnesol (FA) activates glomerulus DC3, with PN terminals that populate the anterior part of the calyx, similarly to VA1d (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an odorant representation database (Münch and Galizia, 2016) and confirmed by EM data visualization.

claim: Pentyl acetate-responding microglomeruli are more prevalent in the posterior part of the calyx compared to methyl palmitate and farnesol.
source: We confirmed this regionalization of activities via volumetric imaging of calyces of MB247-homer::GCaMP3 flies, which showed a prevalence of PA-responding MGs in the posterior part of the calyx, in comparison to MP and FA ones, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, n = 7, p < 0.01 (**) for both PA vs. MP and PA vs. FA in Z1 and Z2, multiple t-tests).
evidence: The claim is supported by volumetric calcium imaging data with statistical testing (n = 7, p < 0.01).

claim: The ratio of APL calcium transients to pentyl acetate and methyl palmitate is highly variable throughout the volume of the calyx.
source: Interestingly, we found the ratio of the calcium transients to be highly inconstant throughout the volume of the calyx for the structurally more distant odours PA and MP (see also Materials and methods for details). In particular, the PA/MP fluorescence ratio was higher in the posterior sections of the calyx and reduced in the anterior ones (Figure 5C, black line), reflecting the bouton distribution of the PNs activated by these two odours.
evidence: The claim is supported by volumetric calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The pentyl acetate/methyl palmitate fluorescence ratio in APL was higher in the posterior sections of the calyx and reduced in the anterior ones.
source: In particular, the PA/MP fluorescence ratio was higher in the posterior sections of the calyx and reduced in the anterior ones (Figure 5C, black line), reflecting the bouton distribution of the PNs activated by these two odours.
evidence: The claim is supported by volumetric calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The fluorescence ratio of farnesol to methyl palmitate in APL was more homogeneous across the calyx volume.
source: By contrast, the fluorescence ratio of FA to MP was more homogeneous across the calyx volume, reflecting the fact that the boutons of the PNs that respond to these odours are located in a similar region of the calyx (Figure 5C, blue line).
evidence: The claim is supported by volumetric calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: APL calcium transients are differently distributed in the calycal volume depending on the odour.
source: In other words, not only APL calcium transients were different with different odours, as already shown (Figure 2), but these transients were also differently distributed in the calycal volume depending on the odour, strengthening the link between structural and functional data.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the spatial distribution of APL responses varies with different odours in a manner consistent with PN bouton distribution.

claim: APL is locally activated in the calyx at the microglomeruli corresponding to activated projection neurons.
source: Combined with the information about synapse distribution, these data suggest that APL is locally activated in the calyx at the MGs corresponding to activated PNs, and that the tone of APL inhibition in the calyx is a gradient that slowly degrades with increasing distance from the active boutons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the spatial correlation between PN bouton distribution and APL calcium transient distribution.

claim: The tone of APL inhibition in the calyx is a gradient that slowly degrades with increasing distance from the active boutons.
source: Combined with the information about synapse distribution, these data suggest that APL is locally activated in the calyx at the MGs corresponding to activated PNs, and that the tone of APL inhibition in the calyx is a gradient that slowly degrades with increasing distance from the active boutons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that APL response ratios vary across the calyx volume in a manner consistent with PN bouton distribution.

claim: APL inhibition onto microglomeruli of the mushroom body calyx shows signs of locality.
source: Taken together, APL inhibition onto MGs of the MB calyx showed signs of locality.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the volumetric imaging data showing spatially variable APL responses corresponding to PN bouton distribution.

claim: Calcium transients in APL's parallel neurites at the mushroom body lobes fail to propagate over long distances.
source: Of notice, a similar spreading mechanism has been observed in APL's parallel neurites at the MB lobes, where calcium transients failed to propagate over long distances (Amin et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Amin et al., 2020.

claim: The inhibitory APL neuron provides inhibition scaled to the projection neurons excitatory inputs to the calyx.
source: Here, we show that the inhibitory APL neuron, by participating in the structure of MGs of the Drosophila MB calyx, provides inhibition scaled to the PNs excitatory inputs to the calyx.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations that APL response correlates with PN input strength and that APL normalizes KC responses.

claim: The average strength and distribution of postsynaptic responses in Kenyon cell dendritic claws become more similar across different odour representations due to APL activity.
source: As a result, the average strength and the distribution of postsynaptic responses in KC dendritic claws become more similar across different odour representations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that KC claw responses are more uniform across odours compared to PN bouton responses, and this uniformity is lost when APL is blocked.

claim: The normalization of postsynaptic responses operated by APL is at the core of pattern separation in the mushroom body.
source: We suggest that this normalization of postsynaptic responses operated by APL is at the core of pattern separation in the MB.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the inference that APL's normalization function supports the sparse coding required for pattern separation.

claim: APL inhibition makes Kenyon cell input integration dependent on the combinatorial pattern of inputs rather than on the strength of individual inputs.
source: Our data suggest that the APL neuron, by confining KC claws responses within a certain range of activation, ensures that KCs requirement of multiple coactive claws is respected even in the presence of highly variable input strengths. In other words, APL inhibition makes KC input integration dependent on the combinatorial pattern of inputs rather than on the strength of individual inputs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that APL normalizes KC responses despite variable PN input strengths.

claim: Blocking APL leads to an increased correspondence between input strength and Kenyon cell response.
source: In support of this, blocking APL leads to an increased correspondence between input strength and KC response.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observation that KC responses in APL OFF conditions resemble PN bouton responses.

claim: GABAergic interneurons in the antennal lobe perform input gain control normalization.
source: Of notice, odour discrimination is achieved at multiple levels of the Drosophila olfactory pathway by different types of inhibitory neurons. Indeed, input gain control normalization has been described for GABAergic interneurons in the AL (Olsen and Wilson, 2008) as well as for inhibitory iPNs at the lateral horn (Parnas et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Olsen and Wilson, 2008.

claim: Inhibitory projection neurons at the lateral horn perform input gain control normalization.
source: Of notice, odour discrimination is achieved at multiple levels of the Drosophila olfactory pathway by different types of inhibitory neurons. Indeed, input gain control normalization has been described for GABAergic interneurons in the AL (Olsen and Wilson, 2008) as well as for inhibitory iPNs at the lateral horn (Parnas et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Parnas et al., 2013.

claim: APL and its homolog GGN in the locust show increased depolarization in response to increasing odour concentration.
source: Additionally, APL and its homolog GGN in the locust showed increased depolarization in response to increasing odour concentration (Papadopoulou et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Papadopoulou et al., 2011.

claim: The normalization performed by APL might be acting not only across stimuli identities, but also among concentrations of the same stimulus.
source: This, combined with our findings, suggests that the normalization performed by APL might be acting not only across stimuli identities, but also among concentrations of the same stimulus.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that APL responds to odour concentration changes and the current findings about normalization across odour identities.

claim: Granule cells receive both feedforward and feedback inhibition from Golgi cells at the cerebellar cortex.
source: For example, granule cells receive both feedforward and feedback inhibition from Golgi cells at the cerebellar cortex (Vos et al., 1999; Duguid et al., 2015), which are driven by excitatory inputs from the mossy fibers (Kanichay and Silver, 2008) and granule cells' axons, respectively (Cesana et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vos et al., 1999 and Duguid et al., 2015.

claim: Golgi cells are driven by excitatory inputs from mossy fibers.
source: For example, granule cells receive both feedforward and feedback inhibition from Golgi cells at the cerebellar cortex (Vos et al., 1999; Duguid et al., 2015), which are driven by excitatory inputs from the mossy fibers (Kanichay and Silver, 2008) and granule cells' axons, respectively (Cesana et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kanichay and Silver, 2008.

claim: Golgi cells are driven by excitatory inputs from granule cells' axons.
source: For example, granule cells receive both feedforward and feedback inhibition from Golgi cells at the cerebellar cortex (Vos et al., 1999; Duguid et al., 2015), which are driven by excitatory inputs from the mossy fibers (Kanichay and Silver, 2008) and granule cells' axons, respectively (Cesana et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cesana et al., 2013.

claim: Golgi cell recruitment scales with mossy fiber input density.
source: Moreover, it has recently been demonstrated that Golgi cells recruit scales with the mossy fibers input density (Tabuchi et al., 2019), similarly to what we observed in our functional imaging experiments.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tabuchi et al., 2019.

claim: Adaptive regulation of Kenyon cells sparseness by feedforward inhibition has been theorized in realistic computational models of insect mushroom bodies.
source: Additionally, adaptive regulation of KCs sparseness by feedforward inhibition has already been theorized in realistic computational models of insect's MBs (Assisi et al., 2007; Luo et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to computational modeling studies (Assisi et al., 2007; Luo et al., 2010).

claim: α/βc Kenyon cells have higher input resistances and longer membrane time constants compared to α'/β' Kenyon cells.
source: For example, α/βc KCs were found to have a higher input resistances and longer membrane time constants compared to α'/β' KCs, resulting in a sigmoidal current-spike frequency function rather than a linear one (Groschner et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Groschner et al., 2018.

claim: α/βc Kenyon cells have a sigmoidal current-spike frequency function rather than a linear one.
source: For example, α/βc KCs were found to have a higher input resistances and longer membrane time constants compared to α'/β' KCs, resulting in a sigmoidal current-spike frequency function rather than a linear one (Groschner et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Groschner et al., 2018.

claim: Golgi cells are responsible for both tonic inhibition, controlling granule cells spike number, and phasic inhibition, limiting the duration of granule cells responses.
source: Additionally, a difference in synapses distribution can also indicate that two inhibitory mechanisms coexist at the MB calyx, similarly to what has been shown in the cerebellum where Golgi cells are responsible for both tonic inhibition, controlling granule cells spike number (Brickley et al., 1996), gain control (Mitchell and Silver, 2003), and phasic inhibition, limiting the duration of granule cells responses (D'Angelo, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brickley et al., 1996; Mitchell and Silver, 2003; D'Angelo, 2009.

claim: Localized APL response has been reported in the Drosophila mushroom body.
source: As a matter of fact, similar examples of localized APL response as described here have been reported in the Drosophila MB (Amin et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019) as well as in the APL's homolog GGN in the locust (Ray et al., 2020; Leitch and Laurent, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Amin et al., 2020 and Wang et al., 2019.

claim: Localized response has been reported in APL's homolog GGN in the locust.
source: As a matter of fact, similar examples of localized APL response as described here have been reported in the Drosophila MB (Amin et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019) as well as in the APL's homolog GGN in the locust (Ray et al., 2020; Leitch and Laurent, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ray et al., 2020 and Leitch and Laurent, 1996.

claim: Local microcircuits allow a single neuron to mimic the activity of several inhibitory interneurons.
source: An advantage of having local microcircuits is that it allows a single neuron to mimic the activity of several inhibitory interneurons, as described in amacrine cells of both mammals (Grimes et al., 2010) and Drosophila (Meier and Borst, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grimes et al., 2010 and Meier and Borst, 2019.

claim: A parallel local-global inhibition is suggested to expand the dynamic range of inputs able to activate Kenyon cells.
source: Additionally, a parallel local-global inhibition is suggested to expand the dynamic range of inputs able to activate KCs (Ray et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ray et al., 2020.

claim: Silencing of the GABAA receptor Rdl in Kenyon cells increased calcium responses in the mushroom body, including the calyx.
source: Accordingly, silencing of the GABAA receptor Rdl in KCs increased calcium responses in the MB, including the calyx (Liu et al., 2007), and reduced sparseness of odour representations (Lei et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2007.

claim: Silencing of the GABAA receptor Rdl in Kenyon cells reduced sparseness of odour representations.
source: Accordingly, silencing of the GABAA receptor Rdl in KCs increased calcium responses in the MB, including the calyx (Liu et al., 2007), and reduced sparseness of odour representations (Lei et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lei et al., 2013.

claim: Reducing GABA synthesis in APL by RNAi has been found to improve olfactory learning.
source: One possible caveat to our hypothesis is given by the fact that reducing GABA synthesis in APL by RNAi has been found to improve olfactory learning (Lei et al., 2013; Liu and Davis, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lei et al., 2013 and Liu and Davis, 2009.

claim: Incomplete silencing of APL via RNAi increases Kenyon cell output without affecting sparseness.
source: Indeed, incomplete silencing via RNAi increases KC output without affecting sparseness, whereas blocking APL output via shibirets leads to large, overlapping odour representations and impaired olfactory discrimination (Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lin et al., 2014.

claim: Blocking APL output via shibirets leads to large, overlapping odour representations and impaired olfactory discrimination.
source: Indeed, incomplete silencing via RNAi increases KC output without affecting sparseness, whereas blocking APL output via shibirets leads to large, overlapping odour representations and impaired olfactory discrimination (Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lin et al., 2014.

claim: Memory consolidation has been associated with structural plasticity in the calyx.
source: In the future, it will be interesting to investigate the impact of APL on memory consolidation, which has been associated with structural plasticity in the calyx (Baltruschat et al., 2021) and with changes in the KC response (Delestro et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Baltruschat et al., 2021.

claim: Memory consolidation has been associated with changes in the Kenyon cell response.
source: In the future, it will be interesting to investigate the impact of APL on memory consolidation, which has been associated with structural plasticity in the calyx (Baltruschat et al., 2021) and with changes in the KC response (Delestro et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Delestro et al., 2020.
